Content:
We've seen how to calculate a particle's velocity and displacement when its acceleration is a function of displacement. In this lesson, we'll use this knowledge to compute various properties of a particle in motion.

Content:
Suppose a particle [MATH: P] moves along the [MATH: x]-axis. Its displacement from the origin is [MATH: x\,\rm{m},] its velocity is [MATH: v\,\rm{m/s},] and its acceleration is [MATH: 2x\,\rm{m/s}^2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e75567efc2ee188928401e31c0d4574a]

Content:
Furthermore, suppose [MATH: P] has velocity [MATH: 2\,\rm{m/s}] when its displacement is [MATH: \sqrt{3}\,\rm{m}.]

Content:
Let's use this information to determine at which values of [MATH: x] the particle is instantaneously at rest.

Content:
Since the acceleration of the particle [MATH: P] is [MATH: 2x\,\rm{m/s}^2,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2x.]

Content:
Using the fact that
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),]
we can rewrite our equation as

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x.]

Content:
Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to [MATH: x,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int 2x \:\textrm{d}x]

Content:
which gives the general solution

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac12v^2 = x^2+ C.]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: v=2\,\rm{m/s}] when [MATH: x=\sqrt 3\,\rm{m},] we can find the value of the constant [MATH: C,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(2)v^{2}|= x^{2} + C; (1)/(2)(2)^{2}|= (sqrt(3))^{2} + C; 2|= 3 + C; C|= − 1]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac12v^2 = x^2-1.]

Content:
Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when [MATH: v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.] We find the displacement of the particle when [MATH: P] is instantaneously at rest by substituting [MATH: v=0] in the equation above and solving for [MATH: x{:}]

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(2)v^{2}|= x^{2} − 1; (1)/(2)(0)^{2}|= x^{2} − 1; x^{2}|= 1; x|= ± 1m]

If [MATH: P] has velocity [MATH: \sqrt2\,\rm{m/s}] when its displacement is [MATH: 1\,\rm{m},] find the value of [MATH: x] for which [MATH: P] is instantaneously at rest.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since the acceleration of the particle [MATH: P] has magnitude [MATH: (2x-2)\,\rm{m/s}^2] and is directed toward [MATH: O,] we have

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -(2x-2).]

Using the fact that [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),] we can rewrite our equation as

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -(2x-2).]

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to [MATH: x,] we have

[MATH: \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x = \int (-2x+2) \:\textrm{d}x]

which gives the general solution

[MATH: \dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x + C.]

Now, since [MATH: v=\sqrt{2}\,\rm{m/s}] when [MATH: x=1\,\rm{m},] we can find the value of the constant [MATH: C,] as follows:

[MATH: (1)/(2)v^{2}|= − x^{2} + 2x + C; (1)/(2)(sqrt(2))^{2}|= − (1)^{2} + 2(1) + C; C|= 1 + 1 − 2; C|= 0]

Therefore,

[MATH: \dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x.]

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when [MATH: v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.] We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting [MATH: v=0] in the equation above and solving for [MATH: x{:}]

[MATH: (1)/(2)v^{2}|= − x^{2} + 2x; (1)/(2)(0)^{2}|= − x^{2} + 2x; x^{2} − 2x|= 0; x(x − 2)|= 0]

The only solution of this equation for [MATH: x \geq 1] is [MATH: x=2\,\rm{m}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We've seen how to calculate a particle's velocity and displacement when its acceleration is a function of displacement. In this lesson, we'll use this knowledge to compute various properties of a particle in motion.

Content:
Suppose a particle [MATH: P] moves along the [MATH: x]-axis. Its displacement from the origin is [MATH: x\,\rm{m},] its velocity is [MATH: v\,\rm{m/s},] and its acceleration is [MATH: 2x\,\rm{m/s}^2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e75567efc2ee188928401e31c0d4574a]

Content:
Furthermore, suppose [MATH: P] has velocity [MATH: 2\,\rm{m/s}] when its displacement is [MATH: \sqrt{3}\,\rm{m}.]

Content:
Let's use this information to determine at which values of [MATH: x] the particle is instantaneously at rest.

Content:
Since the acceleration of the particle [MATH: P] is [MATH: 2x\,\rm{m/s}^2,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2x.]

Content:
Using the fact that
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),]
we can rewrite our equation as

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x.]

Content:
Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to [MATH: x,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int 2x \:\textrm{d}x]

Content:
which gives the general solution

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac12v^2 = x^2+ C.]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: v=2\,\rm{m/s}] when [MATH: x=\sqrt 3\,\rm{m},] we can find the value of the constant [MATH: C,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(2)v^{2}|= x^{2} + C; (1)/(2)(2)^{2}|= (sqrt(3))^{2} + C; 2|= 3 + C; C|= − 1]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac12v^2 = x^2-1.]

Content:
Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when [MATH: v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.] We find the displacement of the particle when [MATH: P] is instantaneously at rest by substituting [MATH: v=0] in the equation above and solving for [MATH: x{:}]

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(2)v^{2}|= x^{2} − 1; (1)/(2)(0)^{2}|= x^{2} − 1; x^{2}|= 1; x|= ± 1m]

Item 2 — Example: Finding Points Where a Particle Is at Instantaneous Rest

Example Prompt:

EXPLANATION

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -(2x-2).]

Using the fact that
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),]
we can rewrite our equation as

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -(2x-2).]

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to [MATH: x,] we have

[MATH: \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int (-2x+2) \:\textrm{d}x]

which gives the general solution

[MATH: \dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x + C.]

[MATH: (1)/(2)v^{2}|= − x^{2} + 2x + C; (1)/(2)(sqrt(2))^{2}|= − (1)^{2} + 2(1) + C; C|= 1 + 1 − 2; C|= 0]

[MATH: \dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x.]
